1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

Leon et al. (2024) demonstrated the ForestSearch methodology using the German Breast Cancer Study Group (GBSG) dataset (survival::gbsg) as both the applied analysis target and the covariate template for simulation studies. The setup_gbsg_dgm() convenience function encodes all GBSG-specific preparation choices — variable discretisation, subgroup definition, Weibull calibration — into a single reproducible call.

This document adapts the same simulation framework to the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 (ACTG175) dataset from the speff2trial package. ACTG175 is a randomised trial of four antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected subjects (Hammer et al., NEJM 1996). Following León et al. (2024, Section 4.2), we compare arm 1 (zidovudine + didanosine, ZDV+ddI) to arm 3 (didanosine alone, ddI) and search for a subgroup with pronounced treatment benefit (\(N = 1{,}083\)).

The adaptation serves two purposes:

  1. Methodological validation: confirming that the ForestSearch operating characteristics generalise beyond the GBSG breast cancer setting to a different disease, population, endpoint structure, and covariate set — and specifically to the benefit-search variant of the algorithm.

  2. Template for new-dataset simulations: demonstrating the recommended workflow when setup_gbsg_dgm() is not appropriate and the analyst must use generate_aft_dgm_flex() directly.

1.2 Benefit Search via Treatment Switching

ForestSearch’s default mode identifies subgroups where treatment is detrimental (hazard ratio \(> 1\)). To identify subgroups with pronounced benefit instead, León et al. (2024, §4.2) introduced a treatment-switching approach:

  1. Switch treatment roles: recode the treatment indicator so that control becomes “treatment” and vice versa. In the ACTG175 context: ddI monotherapy (originally control) is recoded as treat = 1, and ZDV+ddI combination (originally experimental) becomes treat = 0.

  2. Raise the thresholds: under switched roles, a subgroup that strongly benefits from the original treatment will appear to have a high HR (ddI alone is worse for these patients). The paper used:

    • \(c_1 = 1/0.60 \approx 1.667\) (screening: original HR \(\leq 0.60\))
    • \(c_2 = 1/0.80 = 1.25\) (consistency: original HR \(\leq 0.80\))

  3. Run ForestSearch with these thresholds on the switched data. The identified “harm” subgroup \(\hat{H}\) under switched roles is the benefit subgroup \(\hat{Q}\) under the original treatment coding.

  4. Invert the results: hazard ratios reported by ForestSearch are inverted (\(1/\text{HR}\)) to return to the original treatment scale.

In the paper’s analysis, this approach identified \(\hat{Q} = \{\text{Age} > 34 \cap \text{Preanti} \leq 744.5\}\) with a bias-corrected HR of \(0.59\) (\(0.37\), \(0.94\)) — a substantially stronger benefit than the ITT HR of \(0.84\).

The simulation DGM in this document is built on the switched treatment data. All ForestSearch analyses run on the switched indicator. The calibration target HR \(= 2.0\) (under switched treatment) corresponds to an original-scale HR \(= 0.50\), representing a strong treatment benefit in the subgroup.

1.3 Adaptation Checklist

To substitute your own trial data for ACTG175, you must address each of the following steps. The sections that follow implement each one for ACTG175; cross-references are provided so you can see the concrete implementation alongside each checklist item.

Step What to do Section
1. Load your data Create id, y (observed time), event (0/1 indicator), and treat (0 = control, 1 = treatment) columns. Time units for y set the time scale for the entire simulation. Section 2
2. Choose confounders Identify the candidate variables for the subgroup search. These become factor_vars in the DGM and confounders_base in the simulation. Section 2
3. Discretise continuous variables Create binary z1, z2, … columns from continuous covariates. Document your cutpoint rationale (see Section 1.4). Section 2
4. Define the harm subgroup Set dgm_subgroup_vars and dgm_subgroup_cuts consistently with your factor coding. Verify with an explicit stopifnot() check. Section 4
5. Set time-scale parameters Ensure sim_analysis_time is in the same units as your outcome variable. Run the time-scale diagnostic after DGM creation. Section 4
6. Update cox_formula_adj Include confounders appropriate for your study. The formula must use simulated column names (y_sim, event_sim, treat_sim). Setup chunk
7. Update confounders_base This must list all z* variable names passed to ForestSearch and GRF. It must match factor_vars in the DGM call. Section 6
8. Calibrate k_inter Run the grid search targeting a clinically meaningful HR(H). Section 4.3
9. Run time-scale diagnostic Verify exp(dgm$model_params$mu) is close to your observed median event time. Section 4.2.1
10. Run censoring diagnostic Use check_censoring_dgm() to compare simulated vs observed censoring. Section 5.1
11. Set simulation count Use \(\geq 500\) replicates for stable operating characteristics. Section 6

1.4 Choosing Discretisation Cutpoints

ForestSearch operates on binary (factor) covariates. Continuous variables must be discretised before building the DGM. There are three common strategies:

  1. Clinical cutpoints — use thresholds defined by domain knowledge (e.g., CD4 \(< 200\) cells/mm³ for AIDS-defining immunosuppression). Preferred when available.

  2. Data-driven medians — split at the sample median; appropriate when no clinical threshold exists. Used here for z3 (Karnofsky performance score) and z4 (CD4 baseline count).

  3. GRF-guided splits — run a preliminary GRF analysis on the observed data (grf::causal_forest()) to identify the variable-importance-weighted split points that maximise treatment effect heterogeneity. This was the approach for z1 (age \(> 34\)) and z2 (preanti \(\leq 744.5\)), derived from the analysis in actg175_analysis_v1.Rnw.

For your own dataset, we recommend starting with strategy (1) where available, falling back to (2), and optionally using (3) as a sensitivity analysis. Whichever approach you choose, document the rationale alongside the cutpoint value in your setup chunk.

1.5 Steps for Swapping GBSG with ACTG175

Replacing the GBSG template with ACTG175 requires changes at every stage of the simulation pipeline. The table below summarises each change; subsequent sections implement them in detail.

Step GBSG (original) ACTG175 (this document)
Data source survival::gbsg (686 patients) speff2trial::ACTG175, arms 1 vs 3 (~1,083 patients)
Outcome Recurrence-free survival in months (rfstime / 30.4375) Time to first event in months (days / 30.4375)
Event indicator status (1 = recurrence/death) cens (1 = event)
Treatment hormon (0/1) arms: 1 = ZDV+ddI (combination), 3 = ddI (monotherapy); switched for benefit search
Confounders 7 binary variables: ER, age, meno, PgR, nodes, size, grade 12 variables: age, preanti, weight, Karnofsky, CD4, CD8, hemophilia, homosexual, IV drugs, race, gender, symptoms
Discretisation ER \(\leq\) Q25, age \(\leq\) median, meno = premenopausal, etc. Age \(>\) 34, preanti \(\leq\) 744.5, weight \(\leq\) 75 kg, CD4 \(\leq\) median, etc. (from León et al. 2024 analysis)
Subgroup definition H = {ER-low and premenopausal} (~13% prevalence) Q = {Age > 34 and Preanti ≤ 744.5} (~35% prevalence, benefit subgroup)
Censoring Weibull; analysis_time = 84 months Weibull; analysis_time = 48 months ($$4 years)
ForestSearch parameters n.min = 60, maxk = 2, hr.threshold = 1.25 hr.threshold = 1.667, hr.consistency = 1.25 (benefit search thresholds)

The benefit subgroup definition for ACTG175 is derived from the ForestSearch analysis in León et al. (2024, Section 4.2), which identified Age \(> 34\) and prior antiretroviral therapy \(\leq 744.5\) days as the combination defining a subgroup with pronounced treatment benefit (\(\hat{Q}\): HR \(= 0.59\), \(0.37\)–\(0.94\)).

library(forestsearch)

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(gt)
library(foreach)
library(doFuture)
#> Loading required package: future
#>

#>

library(future)

# -- Safe foreach result collection -------------------------------------------
# collect_results() now lives in forestsearch (R/forestsearch_helpers.R).
# Called via ::: since it is an internal (unexported) utility.

2.1 Loading and Preparing Both Datasets

The code below prepares both datasets for the simulation framework. For each dataset, the key steps are:

  1. Create a standardised outcome variable (y) in the dataset’s natural time units.
  2. Create a binary treatment indicator (treat: 0 = control, 1 = treatment).
  3. Discretise continuous covariates into binary factors (z1, z2, …) using the cutpoints defined in the setup chunk.
  4. Construct the true harm-subgroup indicator (flag_harm) using the same variables and levels specified in dgm_subgroup_vars and dgm_subgroup_cuts.
# ── GBSG ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
gbsg_df        <- survival::gbsg
gbsg_df$y      <- gbsg_df$rfstime / 30.4375
gbsg_df$treat  <- gbsg_df$hormon

er_cut         <- quantile(gbsg_df$er, probs = gbsg_er_quantile)
gbsg_df$z1     <- as.factor(ifelse(gbsg_df$er <= er_cut, 1L, 0L))
gbsg_df$z3     <- as.factor(ifelse(gbsg_df$meno == 0, 1L, 0L))
gbsg_df$flag_harm <- as.integer(gbsg_df$z1 == 1 & gbsg_df$z3 == 1)

# ── ACTG175 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Select arms 1 (ZDV+ddI) and 3 (ddI alone), matching the paper
actg_df        <- subset(speff2trial::ACTG175, arms %in% actg_arms)
actg_df$id     <- seq_len(nrow(actg_df))
actg_df$time_days   <- actg_df$days
actg_df$time_months <- actg_df$time_days / 30.4375

# Original treatment coding: arm 1 (ZDV+ddI) = 1, arm 3 (ddI) = 0
actg_df$treat_orig <- ifelse(actg_df$arms == actg_treat_arm, 1L, 0L)

# SWITCHED treatment coding for benefit search:
# ddI (arm 3) = 1 ("treatment"), ZDV+ddI (arm 1) = 0 ("control")
# Under switched roles, ForestSearch's harm-detection machinery
# identifies the BENEFIT subgroup Q.
actg_df$treat  <- 1L - actg_df$treat_orig

cat(sprintf("ACTG175: N = %d (arm 1: n=%d, arm 3: n=%d)\n",
    nrow(actg_df),
    sum(actg_df$treat_orig == 1), sum(actg_df$treat_orig == 0)))
#> ACTG175: N = 1083 (arm 1: n=522, arm 3: n=561)
cat(sprintf("Treatment switched: treat=1 is ddI (original control)\n"))
#> Treatment switched: treat=1 is ddI (original control)
# ── Discretise continuous variables into binary factors ───────
# Subgroup-defining variables (from Leon et al. 2024, Section 4.2):
# z1: age > actg_age_cut  (subgroup factor 1 — older patients)
actg_df$z1  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$age  > actg_age_cut,  1L, 0L))
# z2: preanti <= actg_preanti_cut  (subgroup factor 2 — less prior treatment)
actg_df$z2  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$preanti <= actg_preanti_cut, 1L, 0L))
# z3: weight <= actg_wtkg_cut (prognostic)
actg_df$z3  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$wtkg <= actg_wtkg_cut, 1L, 0L))
# z4: Karnofsky <= median (data-driven cutpoint)
actg_df$z4  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$karnof <= median(actg_df$karnof), 1L, 0L
))
# z5: CD4 baseline <= median (data-driven cutpoint)
actg_df$z5  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$cd40 <= median(actg_df$cd40), 1L, 0L
))
# z6: CD8 <= median (data-driven cutpoint)
actg_df$z6  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$cd80 <= median(actg_df$cd80), 1L, 0L
))
# z7-z12: binary indicators (passed through as-is from the dataset)
actg_df$z7  <- as.factor(actg_df$hemo)
actg_df$z8  <- as.factor(actg_df$homo)
actg_df$z9  <- as.factor(actg_df$drugs)
actg_df$z10 <- as.factor(actg_df$race)
actg_df$z11 <- as.factor(actg_df$gender)
actg_df$z12 <- as.factor(actg_df$symptom)

# ── Realistic analyst-facing candidate set ──────────────────────
# The truly-binary indicators are coerced to factors so forestsearch's
# is.continuous() detection treats them as categorical (no median /
# GRF cut attempted).  The continuous columns (age, preanti, wtkg,
# karnof, cd40, cd80) are left in their RAW numeric form -- the
# search methods discover cuts.  The z1-z12 factors built above
# remain on the data frame only for the DGM (factor_vars argument)
# and the truth flag.
for (v in analysis_binary_vars) {
  actg_df[[v]] <- as.factor(actg_df[[v]])
}
confounders_analysis <- c(analysis_continuous_vars, analysis_binary_vars)

# ── Factor coding summary ──────────────────────────────────────
# z1  = 1 => age > 34          (older — benefit subgroup factor)
# z2  = 1 => preanti <= 744.5  (less prior ART — benefit subgroup factor)
# z3  = 1 => weight <= 75 kg   (low weight)
# z4  = 1 => Karnofsky <= median (lower performance)
# z5  = 1 => CD4 <= median     (lower baseline CD4)
# z6  = 1 => CD8 <= median     (lower CD8)
# z7  = 1 => hemophilia yes
# z8  = 1 => homosexual activity yes
# z9  = 1 => IV drug use yes
# z10 = 1 => non-white
# z11 = 1 => male
# z12 = 1 => symptomatic yes

# ── Benefit subgroup: z1 = 1 AND z2 = 1 ───────────────────────
# Q = {Age > 34 AND Preanti <= 744.5}
# Under switched treatment, Q appears as the "harm" subgroup.
actg_df$flag_harm <- as.integer(
  actg_df[[dgm_subgroup_vars[1]]] == dgm_subgroup_cuts[[dgm_subgroup_vars[1]]] &
  actg_df[[dgm_subgroup_vars[2]]] == dgm_subgroup_cuts[[dgm_subgroup_vars[2]]]
)

# Verify subgroup definition matches expectations
stopifnot(
  identical(dgm_subgroup_vars, c("z1", "z2")),
  identical(dgm_subgroup_cuts, list(z1 = 1L, z2 = 1L))
)
cat(sprintf(
  "Benefit subgroup Q: z1 == 1 (age > %d) AND z2 == 1 (preanti <= %.1f)\n",
  actg_age_cut, actg_preanti_cut
))
#> Benefit subgroup Q: z1 == 1 (age > 34) AND z2 == 1 (preanti <= 744.5)
cat(sprintf(
  "  Q prevalence: %d / %d (%.1f%%)\n",
  sum(actg_df$flag_harm), nrow(actg_df),
  100 * mean(actg_df$flag_harm)
))
#>   Q prevalence: 382 / 1083 (35.3%)

2.4 Survival Curves (Observed Data)

Show code 
# ── GBSG KM ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
km_gbsg    <- survfit(Surv(y, status) ~ treat, data = gbsg_df)
km_gbsg_df <- data.frame(
  time = c(km_gbsg$time[1:km_gbsg$strata[1]],
           km_gbsg$time[(km_gbsg$strata[1] + 1):sum(km_gbsg$strata)]),
  surv = c(km_gbsg$surv[1:km_gbsg$strata[1]],
           km_gbsg$surv[(km_gbsg$strata[1] + 1):sum(km_gbsg$strata)]),
  arm = c(
    rep("Control", km_gbsg$strata[1]),
    rep("Hormonal", km_gbsg$strata[2])
  )
)

p_gbsg <- ggplot(km_gbsg_df, aes(x = time, y = surv, colour = arm)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "GBSG",
    x = "Months", y = "Survival Probability",
    colour = "Treatment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# ── ACTG175 KM ───────────────────────────────────────────────
km_actg <- survfit(Surv(time_months, cens) ~ treat_orig, data = actg_df)
km_actg_df <- data.frame(
  time = c(km_actg$time[1:km_actg$strata[1]],
           km_actg$time[(km_actg$strata[1] + 1):sum(km_actg$strata)]),
  surv = c(km_actg$surv[1:km_actg$strata[1]],
           km_actg$surv[(km_actg$strata[1] + 1):sum(km_actg$strata)]),
  arm = c(
    rep("ddI alone (control)", km_actg$strata[1]),
    rep("ZDV+ddI (experimental)", km_actg$strata[2])
  )
)

p_actg <- ggplot(km_actg_df, aes(x = time, y = surv, colour = arm)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "ACTG175",
    x = "Months", y = "Survival Probability",
    colour = "Treatment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_gbsg + p_actg +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Observed Survival in Source Datasets",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  )

2.5 Subgroup Prevalence and Outcome

cat("=== GBSG: Harm subgroup H = {ER-low AND premenopausal} ===\n")
#> === GBSG: Harm subgroup H = {ER-low AND premenopausal} ===
cat("  N(H):", sum(gbsg_df$flag_harm), "/", nrow(gbsg_df),
    sprintf("(%.1f%%)\n", 100 * mean(gbsg_df$flag_harm)))
#>   N(H): 84 / 686 (12.2%)
fit_gbsg_h <- coxph(
  Surv(y, status) ~ treat,
  data = gbsg_df[gbsg_df$flag_harm == 1, ]
)
cat("  Observed HR(H):",
    round(exp(coef(fit_gbsg_h)), 3), "\n\n")
#>   Observed HR(H): 1.725
cat(sprintf(
  "=== ACTG175: Benefit subgroup Q = {age>%d AND preanti<=%.0f} ===\n",
  actg_age_cut, actg_preanti_cut
))
#> === ACTG175: Benefit subgroup Q = {age>34 AND preanti<=744} ===
cat("  N(Q):", sum(actg_df$flag_harm), "/", nrow(actg_df),
    sprintf("(%.1f%%)\n", 100 * mean(actg_df$flag_harm)))
#>   N(Q): 382 / 1083 (35.3%)
fit_actg_h <- coxph(
  Surv(time_months, cens) ~ treat_orig,
  data = actg_df[actg_df$flag_harm == 1, ]
)
cat("  Observed HR(Q), original scale:",
    round(exp(coef(fit_actg_h)), 3), "\n")
#>   Observed HR(Q), original scale: 0.518
fit_actg_hc <- coxph(
  Surv(time_months, cens) ~ treat_orig,
  data = actg_df[actg_df$flag_harm == 0, ]
)
cat("  Observed HR(Qc), original scale:",
    round(exp(coef(fit_actg_hc)), 3), "\n")
#>   Observed HR(Qc), original scale: 1.054

3 Single-Data Analysis on Observed ACTG175

ImportantReal-data setting: no ground-truth classification

This section analyses the actual ACTG175 data – not a simulated trial. The true benefit subgroup in a real trial is unknown; it is the object the analysis is trying to estimate. We therefore report the subgroup ForestSearch identifies and the resulting arm-specific HRs, but we do not compute classification metrics (sens / spec / PPV) against any reference subgroup – there is no clinical truth to classify against. Classification is only meaningful in the simulation setting of Section 6, where the DGM fixes a known \(Q\).

Before any simulation, run ForestSearch on the actual ACTG175 data with details = TRUE to examine every step of the procedure: LASSO screening, GRF variable importance, candidate enumeration, and bootstrap consistency.

NoteWhat the analysis methods see

The analysis candidate set (passed to forestsearch() / grf.subg.harm.survival() as confounders.name) is:

  • Continuous (6): age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80
  • Binary (6): hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom

The methods discover cuts on the continuous covariates themselves; the TRUE cuts (age \(>\) 34, preanti \(\le\) 744.5) are not provided.

3.3 FS vs GRF Concordance on Observed Data

4 Creating the ACTG175 DGM

Because setup_gbsg_dgm() is specific to the GBSG dataset, we use generate_aft_dgm_flex() directly. This requires the analyst to supply the prepared dataset, specify all modelling choices, and define the subgroup explicitly.

The key function arguments are:

  • data: the prepared analysis dataset with y, event, treat, and all z* factor columns.
  • factor_vars: character vector of all binary confounder names (here, z1–z12). These are used as covariates in the AFT model fitted to the observed data.
  • subgroup_vars / subgroup_cuts: define the harm subgroup \(H\). subgroup_cuts specifies the factor level (here, 1L) that indicates membership.
  • model: "alt" embeds a treatment-by-subgroup interaction; "null" fits a uniform treatment effect (no HTE).
  • k_inter: multiplier on the interaction coefficient (AFT log-time scale). Higher values produce larger HR(H).
  • k_treat: multiplier on the main treatment coefficient. Usually 1.0 (retain the observed ITT effect).
  • n_super: size of the super-population drawn from the fitted AFT model. \(5000\) is sufficient for stable HR estimates.

4.1 Step 1: Prepare the Analysis Dataset

The DGM is built on the switched treatment data so that the benefit subgroup \(Q\) appears as a “harm” subgroup in the standard ForestSearch framework. The treat column in dfa is already the switched indicator (ddI = 1, ZDV+ddI = 0).

# Prepare the ACTG175 data for generate_aft_dgm_flex()
# Column names here must match the *_var arguments below.
# Note: 'treat' is already the SWITCHED indicator from the prep step.
dfa        <- actg_df
dfa$y      <- dfa$time_months # outcome in months (days / 30.4375)
dfa$event  <- dfa$cens        # 1 = event, 0 = censored
# 'treat' is the switched indicator (ddI=1, ZDV+ddI=0)

cat("DGM input data:\n")
#> DGM input data:
cat("  N =", nrow(dfa), "\n")
#>   N = 1083
cat("  treat = 1 (ddI monotherapy):", sum(dfa$treat == 1), "\n")
#>   treat = 1 (ddI monotherapy): 561
cat("  treat = 0 (ZDV+ddI combination):", sum(dfa$treat == 0), "\n")
#>   treat = 0 (ZDV+ddI combination): 522
cat("  (Treatment is SWITCHED for benefit search)\n")
#>   (Treatment is SWITCHED for benefit search)

4.2 Step 2: Build the DGM (Alternative Hypothesis)

  data            = dfa,
  outcome_var     = "y",
  event_var       = "event",
  treatment_var   = "treat",
  continuous_vars = dgm_continuous_vars,
  factor_vars     = dgm_factor_vars,
  subgroup_vars   = dgm_subgroup_vars,
  subgroup_cuts   = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
  model           = "alt",
  k_inter         = dgm_k_inter_init,
  k_treat         = dgm_k_treat,

)

4.2.1 Time-Scale Sanity Check

The single most common simulation failure is building the DGM on one time scale (e.g., months) and then passing analysis_time in a different scale. This results in a follow-up window far shorter or longer than the DGM event-time distribution, producing either universal censoring or no censoring at all.

The diagnostic below verifies that the DGM’s implied median event time (exp(mu)) is in the same ballpark as the observed data and that analysis_time is on the correct scale.

# ── KM-based median (handles censoring correctly) ────────────────
# The naive median(dfa$y[dfa$event == 1]) is biased downward because
# subjects with longer true event times are disproportionately
# censored and never enter the event == 1 subset.  The Kaplan-Meier
# estimator accounts for censoring and returns NA when the median is
# not reached within follow-up.
sf_obs <- survival::survfit(survival::Surv(y, event) ~ 1, data = dfa)
km_summary       <- summary(sf_obs)$table
observed_median  <- km_summary[["median"]]
dgm_median       <- exp(dgm_alt$model_params$mu)

if (is.na(observed_median)) {
  # Median not reached within follow-up — common when censoring is
  # heavy.  Fall back to the 25th-percentile event time, which is
  # almost always estimable, and report it as a less-stringent
  # sanity check.
  km_quantiles    <- quantile(sf_obs, probs = 0.25)$quantile
  observed_q25    <- km_quantiles[["25"]]
  cat(sprintf(
    "Observed median event time (KM):  not reached within follow-up\n"))
  cat(sprintf(
    "Observed 25th percentile (KM):    %.1f months\n", observed_q25))
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "Observed median event time (KM):  %.1f months\n", observed_median))
}
#> Observed median event time (KM):  not reached within follow-up
#> Observed 25th percentile (KM):    NA months
cat(sprintf("DGM implied median (exp(mu)):     %.1f months\n", dgm_median))
#> DGM implied median (exp(mu)):     85.5 months
cat(sprintf("analysis_time:                    %.0f months\n", sim_analysis_time))
#> analysis_time:                    48 months
if (sim_analysis_time < dgm_median * 0.5) {
  warning("analysis_time is much shorter than DGM median -- ",
          "expect heavy administrative censoring!")
}
if (sim_analysis_time > dgm_median * 10) {
  warning("analysis_time is much longer than DGM median -- ",
          "nearly all events will be observed (minimal censoring).")
}

4.3 Step 3: Calibrate for Target HR

4.3.1 Why calibrate?

The DGM’s k_inter parameter controls the strength of the treatment-by-subgroup interaction on the AFT (log-time) scale. Because the mapping from k_inter to the Cox-model hazard ratio HR(H) is non-linear and depends on the specific covariate distribution, censoring structure, and baseline hazard, we cannot set k_inter analytically to achieve a desired HR(H). Instead, we search over a grid of candidate values and select the one that yields an HR(H) closest to the target.

A target HR(H) of 2 is used here because it represents a clinically meaningful level of harm — treatment doubles the hazard in the subgroup — and matches the simulation scenarios in León et al. (2024). Users should choose their target based on the effect size they want their simulation to be powered to detect.

Note: calibrate_k_inter() automates this process for GBSG-based DGMs. For non-GBSG datasets, the manual grid search shown here is required. This is a known limitation and will be addressed in a future release.

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()[3]

cal_results <- data.frame(
  k_inter = cal_k_grid,
  hr_H    = NA_real_,
  hr_Hc   = NA_real_,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (i in seq_along(cal_k_grid)) {
  dgm_k <- tryCatch(
    generate_aft_dgm_flex(
      data            = dfa,
      outcome_var     = "y",
      event_var       = "event",
      treatment_var   = "treat",
      continuous_vars = dgm_continuous_vars,
      factor_vars     = dgm_factor_vars,
      subgroup_vars   = dgm_subgroup_vars,
      subgroup_cuts   = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
      model           = "alt",
      k_inter         = cal_k_grid[i],
      k_treat         = dgm_k_treat,
      n_super         = dgm_n_super,
      seed            = sim_seed,
      verbose         = FALSE
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  if (!is.null(dgm_k)) {
    cal_results$hr_H[i]  <- dgm_k$hazard_ratios$harm_subgroup
    cal_results$hr_Hc[i] <- dgm_k$hazard_ratios$no_harm_subgroup
  }
}

# Find k_inter closest to target
cal_valid  <- cal_results[!is.na(cal_results$hr_H), ]
best_idx   <- which.min(abs(cal_valid$hr_H - cal_target_hr))
k_inter_best <- cal_valid$k_inter[best_idx]

cat(sprintf(
  "Calibration: k_inter = %.2f gives HR(H) = %.3f (target: %.1f)\n",
  k_inter_best, cal_valid$hr_H[best_idx], cal_target_hr
))
#> Calibration: k_inter = 2.25 gives HR(H) = 2.043 (target: 2.0)
Show code 
timings$calibrate <- proc.time()[3] - t0
Show code 
ggplot(cal_valid, aes(x = k_inter)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = hr_H,  colour = "HR(H)"),  linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = hr_Hc, colour = "HR(Hc)"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = cal_target_hr, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.0, linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(
    data = cal_valid[best_idx, ],
    aes(x = k_inter, y = hr_H),
    colour = "red", size = 4, shape = 16
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("HR(H)" = "firebrick", "HR(Hc)" = "steelblue")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "k_inter",
    y = "Hazard Ratio",
    title = "ACTG175 DGM Calibration",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "Best: k_inter = %.2f -> HR(H) = %.3f (target: %.1f)",

    ),
    colour = NULL
  ) +

        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

4.5 Step 5: Create Null DGM

Under model = "null", the treatment effect is homogeneous across all patients — no treatment effect heterogeneity. Treatment is still beneficial for everyone; there is simply no subgroup with a different treatment effect. Any subgroup detected under the null is a false positive.

By default, k_treat = 1 preserves the fitted ITT treatment effect. For the benefit-search / switched-treatment setup here, the fitted switched-scale ITT HR is the reciprocal of the original beneficial HR. If the original HR = 0.84, the switched HR = 1/0.84 = 1.19. This sits below the threshold (c1 = 1.667) but the gap is narrower than in harm-search scenarios. The default behaviour (preserved fitted ITT effect) is the conservative, realistic choice; the \(L_\text{eff}\) calibration procedure accounts for this when selecting thresholds.

NoteOptional: widen the gap from c1 with null_target_hr

If you want to study type-I-error inflation in isolation of the proximity to c1, you can target a specific switched-scale ITT HR for the null DGM by setting null_target_hr in the setup chunk. The code below solves for the k_treat value that produces the requested target.

The solver is approximate: k_treat multiplies the AFT log-time treatment coefficient, but the realised Cox HR also depends on the censoring distribution and the covariate distribution, so the constructed HR will be close to but not exactly equal to null_target_hr. After construction we re-check the realised ITT HR; if it is materially off, iterate.

This is not a different research question – the topic remains differential treatment effects across subgroups. It is simply a way to widen the gap between the marginal ITT HR and c1 so that the FPR you measure is driven by search-space multiplicity rather than by the marginal signal sitting close to the detection threshold.

Setting null_target_hr = NULL (the default) preserves the fitted ITT effect (k_treat = 1).

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()[3]

# ── Solve for k_treat under the optional null_target_hr ──────────
# The default keeps k_treat = dgm_k_treat (typically 1.0, preserving
# the fitted ITT effect).  When null_target_hr is non-NULL, we solve:
#   k_treat_null = log(target_hr_switched) / log(fitted_hr_switched)
# fitted_hr_switched comes from the alt DGM's overall hazard ratio,
# which is on the switched scale by construction in this vignette.
dgm_k_treat_null <- dgm_k_treat
if (!is.null(null_target_hr)) {
  fitted_log_hr <- log(dgm_alt$hazard_ratios$overall)
  if (abs(fitted_log_hr) < 1e-8) {
    stop("Fitted ITT log-HR is ~0; cannot rescale to a target HR. ",
         "Leave null_target_hr = NULL.")
  }
  dgm_k_treat_null <- log(null_target_hr) / fitted_log_hr
  message(sprintf(
    "null_target_hr = %.3f  -->  k_treat (null) = %.3f  (fitted log-HR = %.3f)",
    null_target_hr, dgm_k_treat_null, fitted_log_hr))
}

dgm_null <- generate_aft_dgm_flex(
  data            = dfa,
  outcome_var     = "y",
  event_var       = "event",
  treatment_var   = "treat",
  continuous_vars = dgm_continuous_vars,
  factor_vars     = dgm_factor_vars,
  subgroup_vars   = dgm_subgroup_vars,
  subgroup_cuts   = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
  model           = "null",
  k_treat         = dgm_k_treat_null,
  n_super         = dgm_n_super,
  seed            = sim_seed,
  verbose         = TRUE
)

4.5.1 Illustrative k_treat values: HR(ITT) and gap to c1

To give the reader a concrete sense of how k_treat controls the marginal ITT effect and therefore the gap from c1, the table below constructs three illustrative null DGMs at k_treat \(\in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5\}\) using the same data, factor lists, super-population size, and seed as the main dgm_null above. The default (k_treat = 1.0) preserves the fitted ITT effect; larger k_treat amplifies the marginal benefit, pushing the switched-scale HR further above 1 and narrowing the gap to c1; smaller k_treat attenuates the marginal effect toward HR \(\approx 1\) and widens the gap.

Build three illustrative null DGMs and tabulate (click to expand) 
# Three illustrative null DGMs.  These are NOT used in the simulation
# loop below; the simulation uses `dgm_null` from the previous chunk
# (constructed with k_treat = dgm_k_treat_null).  The grid here is
# purely a didactic table so the reader can see how k_treat moves
# HR(ITT) and the gap to c1.
k_treat_grid <- c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5)

illust_rows <- lapply(k_treat_grid, function(k) {
  d <- generate_aft_dgm_flex(
    data            = dfa,
    outcome_var     = "y",
    event_var       = "event",
    treatment_var   = "treat",
    continuous_vars = dgm_continuous_vars,
    factor_vars     = dgm_factor_vars,
    subgroup_vars   = dgm_subgroup_vars,
    subgroup_cuts   = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
    model           = "null",
    k_treat         = k,
    n_super         = dgm_n_super,
    seed            = sim_seed,
    verbose         = FALSE
  )
  d <- add_compat_aliases(d)
  hr_switched <- as.numeric(d$hazard_ratios$overall)
  data.frame(
    k_treat     = k,
    hr_switched = hr_switched,
    hr_original = 1 / hr_switched,
    gap_to_c1   = fs_hr_threshold - hr_switched
  )
})
illust_tbl <- do.call(rbind, illust_rows)

gt::gt(illust_tbl) |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title    = "Illustrative null DGMs: HR(ITT) and gap to c1 by k_treat",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "ACTG175 benefit search, switched scale; c1 = %.3f, n_super = %d",
      fs_hr_threshold, dgm_n_super
    )
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    k_treat     = "k_treat",
    hr_switched = "HR(ITT, switched)",
    hr_original = "HR(ITT, original)",
    gap_to_c1   = gt::md("Gap (c1 \u2212 HR_switched)")
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns  = c(hr_switched, hr_original, gap_to_c1),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = k_treat, decimals = 1) |>
  gt::tab_style(
    style    = gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = k_treat == 1.0)
  ) |>
  gt::tab_footnote(
    footnote = paste0(
      "k_treat = 1.0 (bold row) preserves the fitted ITT effect; this is ",
      "the default null DGM. Smaller k_treat attenuates the marginal ",
      "effect toward HR \u2248 1 (widening the gap to c1); larger k_treat ",
      "amplifies the effect (narrowing the gap). The realised HR is ",
      "approximate -- the AFT log-time scaling does not map exactly to ",
      "the Cox HR, which also depends on the censoring and covariate ",
      "distributions."
    )
  )

5 Single Trial Simulation

Before running the full simulation study, we generate a single simulated trial to verify that the pipeline produces sensible data. This is a useful sanity check: the simulated event rate, subgroup prevalence, and ITT HR should be broadly consistent with the DGM parameters.

Show code 
sim_data <- simulate_from_dgm(
  dgm           = dgm_calibrated,
  n             = single_n,
  rand_ratio    = single_rand_ratio,
  seed          = single_seed,
  analysis_time = sim_analysis_time,
  cens_adjust   = sim_cens_adjust
)

cat("Simulated ACTG175 trial:\n")
#> Simulated ACTG175 trial:
Show code

#>   N = 1000
Show code

    sprintf("(%.1f%%)\n", 100 * mean(sim_data$event_sim)))
#>   Events = 200 (20.0%)
Show code

    sprintf("(%.1f%%)\n", 100 * mean(sim_data$flag_harm)))

Show code

cat("  Estimated ITT HR =", round(exp(coef(fit_sim)), 3), "\n")
#>   Estimated ITT HR = 1.85

5.1 Censoring Diagnostic

The check_censoring_dgm() function compares the simulated censoring distribution against the observed data used to build the DGM. Large discrepancies suggest a time-scale mismatch or a poorly calibrated censoring model.

Show code 
check_censoring_dgm(
  sim_data = sim_data,
  dgm      = dgm_calibrated
)

    exp(coef(fit_sim_adj)["treat_sim"])))
#>   Adjusted HR:   1.849 (z1 + z2 + z3)

5.4 ForestSearch on Simulated Trial

WarningSingle-replicate caveat: realistic-analysis variance

Because the analysis methods see covariates in their RAW form (not the discretised z-factors), variable-screening steps such as LASSO and GRF must rediscover the truth-defining variables from scratch in each replicate. Under modest sample sizes (n = 1000 per trial here), it is expected that any single replicate may fail to retain the true subgroup-defining variables – this is the price of the realistic-analysis pattern, not a bug.

Reliable inference about the method’s behaviour comes from the full simulation loop in Section 7, where the operating characteristics aggregate across 50 simulations. The H1 detection rate, classification metrics, and bias diagnostics in Section 7.2 are the appropriate basis for evaluating the method; the single-replicate output below is a pipeline-sanity check, not a performance claim.

6 Running Simulation Studies

6.1 Setup

plan(multisession, workers = n_workers)
cat("Using", n_workers, "parallel workers\n")
#> Using 12 parallel workers
# ── Candidate variable set ────────────────────────────────────
# confounders_base tells run_simulation_analysis() which columns in
# the simulated data to pass to ForestSearch and GRF as candidate
# subgroup-defining variables.  Mirrors the binary vignette: a real
# analyst would NOT know which variables define Q nor where to cut
# them, so the candidate set is the RAW continuous columns
# (age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80) plus the truly-binary
# factor columns (hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom).  The
# discretised z1-z12 columns remain on the simulated data frame
# only for the DGM (via factor_vars) and the truth flag --- they
# are NOT candidates for the analysis search.
confounders_actg <- confounders_analysis

# ── ForestSearch parameters ───────────────────────────────────
# These are passed to run_simulation_analysis() and forwarded to
# forestsearch().  The annotations below explain each parameter
# and when you might change it for your own study.
fs_params <- list(
  # Column name mappings — must match simulate_from_dgm() output
  outcome.name           = "y_sim",
  event.name             = "event_sim",
  treat.name             = "treat_sim",
  id.name                = "id",

  # Variable screening flags
  use_lasso              = TRUE,    # LASSO pre-screening (recommended)
  use_grf                = TRUE,    # GRF pre-screening (recommended)

  # Subgroup detection thresholds (see Leon et al. 2024, Section 3)
  # c1: a candidate subgroup must have HR > hr.threshold to be flagged.
  # Increase for more conservative detection; decrease for more power.
  hr.threshold           = fs_hr_threshold,
  # c2: in each bootstrap replicate, the subgroup HR must exceed this
  # value.  Typically set to 1.0 (any harm signal).
  hr.consistency         = fs_hr_consistency,
  # The proportion of bootstrap replicates in which the subgroup HR
  # exceeds c2.  The paper default is 0.90.
  pconsistency.threshold = fs_pconsistency_thresh,

  # Computational and sample-size constraints
  fs.splits              = fs_splits,    # Bootstrap replicates (400 is default)
  n.min                  = fs_n_min,     # Minimum subgroup size (both arms)
  d0.min                 = fs_d0_min,    # Minimum events, control arm
  d1.min                 = fs_d1_min,    # Minimum events, treatment arm
  maxk                   = fs_maxk,      # Max subgroup-defining variables
  by.risk                = fs_by_risk,   # Risk-table granularity (time units)
  vi.grf.min             = fs_vi_grf_min, # GRF variable importance threshold
  seedit                 = sim_seed,      # Reproducible split-half consistency

  # Two-stage estimation: after identifying a subgroup, re-estimates
  # the treatment effect using an independent hold-out sample.
  # Recommended for bias correction.
  use_twostage           = TRUE,
  twostage_args          = list(),

  # GRF tuning (applies to ForestSearch's internal GRF pre-screening)
  tune_grf               = grf_tune,

  # Inner parallelism: ForestSearch runs sequentially within each
  # worker.  The outer loop (foreach) parallelises across replicates.
  parallel_args          = list(
    plan = "sequential", workers = 1, show_message = FALSE
  )
)

# -- GRF standalone parameter overrides ----------------------------------------
grf_params <- list(
  dmin.grf     = grf_dmin,
  frac.tau     = grf_frac_tau,
  maxdepth     = grf_maxdepth,
  sg.criterion = grf_sg_criterion,
  tune_grf     = grf_tune
)

# ── Simulation configuration ─────────────────────────────────
sim_config <- list(
  n_sample      = sim_n_sample,
  analysis_time = sim_analysis_time,
  cens_adjust   = sim_cens_adjust
)

7 Results

7.1 Metrics Glossary

The operating-characteristics tables below report three groups of metrics:

  • detection: the proportion of simulations where ForestSearch (or GRF) identifies any subgroup (\(\texttt{any.H} = 1\)). Under the alternative, this is detection power; under the null, it is the false-positive rate (type I error).

  • classification: among simulations where a subgroup was detected, how well the identified subgroup \(\hat{H}\) overlaps with the true subgroup \(H\). Includes sensitivity (proportion of true \(H\) members captured), specificity (proportion of \(H^c\) members correctly excluded), and positive predictive value (PPV, proportion of \(\hat{H}\) that truly belongs to \(H\)).

  • cde_estimates: bias and root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the controlled direct effect (CDE) estimator for the treatment effect within \(\hat{H}\) and \(\hat{H}^c\), relative to the true DGM values. The CDE is defined at the individual level via potential outcomes and represents the causal estimand (see León et al. 2024, Section 2.2).

7.2 Operating Characteristics Under H1

The simulation engine runs on the switched treatment scale. When subgroup_notation = "benefit" is passed to the table functions, they automatically invert all hazard ratios to the original scale (HR < 1 = benefit from ZDV+ddI) and apply Q/Qc notation.

NoteTrimming Cox-HR plug-in columns for the estimation tables

The plug-in Cox HR estimates (hr.H.hat, hr.Hc.hat) can blow up in single replicates where the identified subgroup – typically \(Q^c\) – has zero events in one arm. When that happens the Cox coefficient is unbounded and the realised HR is effectively \(0\) or \(\infty\) on the switched scale, which after inversion to the benefit scale produces extreme display values that swamp the table’s Avg, SD, and Max columns even when the AHR-based columns (ahr.H.hat, ahr.Hc.hat) and bias-corrected columns (hr.H.bc, hr.Hc.bc) remain well-behaved.

Because the package’s existing trimming infrastructure (SGplot_estimates(trim_fraction = ...)) is plumbed only into the violin plotter and not into build_estimation_table(), we apply a symmetric quantile-based winsorization to the four Cox-HR columns at the vignette level on the switched scale, before passing the results to the table functions. AHR columns are left untouched.

Set trim_fraction <- NULL below to disable; the table will then show raw (untrimmed) statistics. The default of 0.01 clamps the bottom and top 1% of values per column.

Trimming helper (click to expand) 
# Symmetric quantile winsorization of Cox-HR plug-in columns.
# Operates on the SWITCHED scale (the columns as stored in
# `results_alt` / `results_null` -- inversion to the benefit scale
# happens inside build_estimation_table()).
#
# Returns a copy of `results` with trimmed values and a "trim_log"
# attribute summarising n_trimmed per column.
winsorize_hr_columns <- function(results,
                                 trim_fraction = 0.01,
                                 cols = c("hr.H.hat", "hr.Hc.hat",
                                          "hr.H.bc",  "hr.Hc.bc")) {
  if (is.null(trim_fraction) || trim_fraction <= 0) {
    return(results)
  }
  if (trim_fraction >= 0.5) {
    stop("trim_fraction must be < 0.5")
  }
  out <- as.data.frame(results)
  trim_log <- data.frame(column = character(0), n_trimmed = integer(0),
                         lower = numeric(0), upper = numeric(0),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  for (col in intersect(cols, names(out))) {
    v <- out[[col]]
    finite_idx <- is.finite(v)
    if (sum(finite_idx) < 5L) next
    lo <- stats::quantile(v[finite_idx], trim_fraction,    na.rm = TRUE)
    hi <- stats::quantile(v[finite_idx], 1 - trim_fraction, na.rm = TRUE)
    flag <- finite_idx & (v < lo | v > hi)
    out[[col]][flag & v < lo] <- lo
    out[[col]][flag & v > hi] <- hi
    trim_log <- rbind(trim_log, data.frame(
      column     = col,
      n_trimmed  = sum(flag, na.rm = TRUE),
      lower      = as.numeric(lo),
      upper      = as.numeric(hi),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
  attr(out, "trim_log") <- trim_log
  out
}

# Apply to both result sets.  The trimmed versions are passed to
# build_estimation_table() below; format_oc_results() uses the
# untrimmed versions because it summarises detection / classification
# (not effect-size summaries).

results_null_trimmed <- winsorize_hr_columns(results_null, trim_fraction)

7.2.1 Interpretation

Show code 
interpret_estimation_table(
  results_alt_trimmed, dgm_calibrated,
  analysis_method = "FS",
  scenario = "alt",
  subgroup_notation = "benefit"
)

Under the alternative hypothesis (true Cox HR(Q) = 0.49, true Cox HR(Qc) = 0.9), 48 of 50 simulations (96.0%) identified a subgroup using FS. The identified subgroup averaged 214 patients (complement: 786).

The naive Cox HR in the identified subgroup averaged 0.34 (SD = 0.07), corresponding to -30.4% relative bias versus the true Cox HR(Q) = 0.49. In the complement, the estimate averaged 0.83 (-7.6% bias vs. true Cox HR(Qc) = 0.9).

Relative to the controlled direct effect (CDE) truth theta-ddagger(Q) = 0.43, the naive plugin shows -21.4% relative bias.

The average hazard ratio (AHR) in the identified subgroup averaged 0.62 (42.4% relative bias vs. true AHR(Q) = 0.43); in the complement, 0.72 (-18.7% bias vs. true AHR(Qc) = 0.89).

7.5 Distribution of Identified Subgroups

The distribution of the identified subgroup \(\hat H\) under H1 (calibrated HTE) and H0 (null) is rendered by forestsearch::plot_sg_distribution(). Under the benefit search, the expected H1 anchor is the DGM’s \(Q = \{\texttt{z1} = 1\} \cap \{\texttt{z2} = 1\}\) (age > 34 and preanti \(\le\) 744.5). Charts adapt their height to the number of bars via sgdist_fig_height() and auto-halve the percentage threshold (up to twice) when no label clears the initial value.

Build subgroup-distribution plots (click to expand) 
plot_sgdist_alt <- plot_sg_distribution(
  results              = results_alt[results_alt$analysis == "FS", ],
  any_col              = "any.H",
  label_col            = "sg.def",

8 Theoretical Detection Probability

The detection probability is the theoretical power of ForestSearch’s bootstrap consistency rule to flag a subgroup with a given HR, given the expected subgroup size and censoring proportion. This curve provides a reference for interpreting the empirical detection rate observed in the simulation.

The method = "cubature" argument uses numerical integration (via the cubature package) to compute the joint probability that the subgroup HR exceeds hr.threshold (c1) and that the proportion of bootstrap replicates exceeding hr.consistency (c2) is at least pconsistency.threshold. An alternative method = "normal" uses a normal approximation.

Show code 
n_sg_expected <- sim_config$n_sample *
  mean(dgm_calibrated$df_super$flag_harm)
prop_cens <- mean(results_alt$p.cens)

cat("Expected subgroup size:", round(n_sg_expected), "\n")
#> Expected subgroup size: 345
Show code 
cat("Censoring proportion:",   round(prop_cens, 3), "\n")
#> Censoring proportion: 0.792
Show code 
cat("True HR(H):",             round(dgm_calibrated$hazard_ratios$harm_subgroup, 3), "\n")
#> True HR(H): 2.043
Show code 
prob_detect <- compute_detection_probability(
  theta          = dgm_calibrated$hazard_ratios$harm_subgroup,
  n_sg           = round(n_sg_expected),
  prop_cens      = prop_cens,
  hr_threshold   = fs_params$hr.threshold,
  hr_consistency = fs_params$hr.consistency,
  method         = "cubature"
)

cat("\nTheoretical P(detect):", round(prob_detect, 3), "\n")
#>

10 Discussion

10.1 Key Differences from the GBSG Simulation

The ACTG175 dataset introduces several features that test ForestSearch under different conditions than the GBSG template:

  1. Larger sample size (\(N \approx 1{,}000\) vs \(686\)): more candidate subgroups survive the n.min filter, potentially increasing \(L_{\text{eff}}\) and the procedure-level FPR.

  2. More confounders (\(12\) vs \(7\)): the combinatorial search space is larger, testing GRF and LASSO screening effectiveness.

  3. Different event rate: ACTG175 has a lower event rate than GBSG, which reduces \(d_{\text{eff}}\) per subgroup and may affect detection power.

  4. Different subgroup structure: the age \(\times\) preanti subgroup is defined by continuous variables discretised at clinically motivated cutpoints, rather than the GBSG’s receptor-status \(\times\) menopausal-status interaction.

  5. Time scale: ACTG175 times have been converted from days to months for AFT model parametrisation but not the HR-scale operating characteristics.

10.2 Reloading Saved Results

When save_results = TRUE, the simulation bundle is saved as an .rds file in the _data/ directory. To reload for downstream analysis:

bundle <- readRDS("_data/actg175_survival_benefit_simulations_50alts_50nulls.rds")

# Core results (data.tables)
results_alt  <- bundle$results_alt
results_null <- bundle$results_null

# DGM objects (class "aft_dgm_flex")
dgm_cal  <- bundle$dgm_calibrated
dgm_null <- bundle$dgm_null

# True effects
bundle$true_effects$hr_Q     # HR(Q) on switched scale
bundle$true_effects$ahr_Q    # AHR(Q)
bundle$true_effects$k_inter  # calibrated interaction multiplier

# Reproduce tables
format_oc_results(results_alt, subgroup_notation = "benefit", ...)
build_estimation_table(results_alt, dgm = dgm_cal,
                       subgroup_notation = "benefit", ...)

10.3 Limitations

  • The ACTG175 benefit subgroup definition (age \(> 34\) AND preanti \(\leq 744.5\)) is based on the exploratory analysis in León et al. (2024, §4.2). The true treatment effect heterogeneity pattern in ACTG175 is unknown.

  • The benefit-search approach (treatment switching) adds a layer of indirection: all DGM, simulation, and ForestSearch operations use the switched treatment indicator, and results must be inverted for interpretation on the original treatment scale.

  • generate_aft_dgm_flex() requires more analyst judgment than setup_gbsg_dgm(). The variable discretisation, subgroup definition, and censoring calibration must all be specified manually.

  • The simulation count (50 sims) is for demonstration. Production studies should use \(\geq 500\) simulations for stable operating characteristics (Monte Carlo SE for a 50% rate \(\approx 2.2\%\) at 500 sims).

  • The adjusted Cox formula (cox_formula_adj) includes only 3 of 12 confounders. This is a deliberate choice for parsimony, but users should select confounders appropriate for their study design.

  • calibrate_k_inter() does not yet support non-GBSG datasets; the manual grid search in Section 4.3 is the current workaround.

```{r setup}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", fig.align = "center")

# ── Simulation control ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Demonstration run; increase to >= 500 for stable operating
# characteristics.  Monte Carlo SE for a 50% detection rate is
# approximately 2.2% at 500 sims and 1.0% at 2500 sims.
nsims_alt   <- 50L
nsims_null  <- 200L

# These are "production" run projection nsims
prod_alt  <- 10000L
prod_null <- 20000L
# 10k/20k ~ 1hr linux

sim_seed    <- 8316951L
n_workers   <- max(1L, floor(0.90 * parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)))

# ── Dataset preparation: GBSG ───────────────────────────────────
gbsg_er_quantile <- 0.25          # ER percentile cutpoint for ER-low definition

# ── Dataset preparation: ACTG175 ───────────────────────────────
#
# ARMS (matching Leon et al. 2024, Section 4.2):
#   speff2trial::ACTG175 arm coding:
#     0 = zidovudine (ZDV) alone
#     1 = ZDV + didanosine (ZDV+ddI)   <- experimental
#     2 = ZDV + zalcitabine (ZDV+ddC)
#     3 = didanosine (ddI) alone        <- control
#
# The paper compared arm 1 (ZDV+ddI, combination) vs arm 3 (ddI,
# monotherapy) and searched for a BENEFIT subgroup Q by switching
# treatment roles.
#
# Cutpoint rationale (from Leon et al. 2024, Section 4.2):
#   z1 (age):     age > 34    — median split; paper found Age > 34
#   z2 (preanti): preanti <= 744.5 — q3 split; paper found Preanti <= q3
#   z3 (wtkg):    wtkg <= 75  — GRF-identified prognostic split
#   z4 (Karnofsky): data-driven median
#   z5 (CD4):     cd40 <= median
#   z6 (CD8):     cd80 <= median
#   z7–z12:       binary indicators passed through as-is
#
actg_arms        <- c(1L, 3L)    # ZDV+ddI (arm 1) vs ddI alone (arm 3)
actg_treat_arm   <- 1L           # Arm coded as treatment = 1 (ZDV+ddI)
actg_age_cut     <- 34           # Age cutpoint (years): age > cut -> z1 = 1
actg_preanti_cut <- 744.5        # Preanti cutpoint (days, q3): preanti <= cut -> z2 = 1
actg_wtkg_cut    <- 75           # Weight cutpoint (kg): wtkg <= cut -> z3 = 1
# z4–z6 use data-driven medians; z7–z12 are binary indicators

# ── Benefit search via treatment switching ─────────────────────
# Leon et al. (2024) searched for benefit by SWITCHING treatment
# roles: the combination (ZDV+ddI) was recoded as control and the
# monotherapy (ddI) as treatment.  Under switched roles, the
# BENEFIT subgroup Q appears as a "harm" subgroup (ddI monotherapy
# is worse than combination for these patients).
#
# ForestSearch then runs with elevated thresholds:
#   c1 = 1/0.60 ≈ 1.667  (screening: HR ≥ 1.667 under switched roles
#                          = HR ≤ 0.60 under original roles)
#   c2 = 1/0.80 = 1.25   (consistency: each split HR ≥ 1.25
#                          = HR ≤ 0.80 under original roles)
#
# After identification, hazard ratios are inverted back to the
# original treatment scale.

# ── DGM construction ────────────────────────────────────────────
# The DGM is built on the SWITCHED treatment data so that the
# benefit subgroup Q appears as a harm subgroup in the DGM
# framework.  All downstream simulation and analysis uses the
# switched treatment indicator.
#
# The DGM uses the discretised z1-z12 factor formulation because
# generate_aft_dgm_flex() requires factor covariates.  The TRUE
# benefit subgroup is defined by {z1 = 1 AND z2 = 1}, i.e.
# age > 34 AND preanti <= 744.5.  This provides the ground truth
# for the sensitivity / PPV computations in run_simulation_analysis()
# but is NOT exposed to the analysis methods (see analysis_*_vars
# below).
dgm_factor_vars   <- paste0("z", 1:12) # All binary confounder names
dgm_continuous_vars <- character(0)    # No continuous covariates
dgm_subgroup_vars <- c("z1", "z2")    # Variables defining benefit subgroup Q
# Within-level values that define membership in Q (under switched treatment,
# Q appears as "harm"):
#   z1 = 1 means age > actg_age_cut   (older, per paper's finding)
#   z2 = 1 means preanti <= actg_preanti_cut (less prior treatment)
dgm_subgroup_cuts <- list(z1 = 1L, z2 = 1L)
dgm_k_treat       <- 1.0             # Main treatment effect multiplier
dgm_n_super       <- 5000L           # Super-population size for DGM
dgm_k_inter_init  <- 2.0             # Starting k_inter before calibration

# ── Null-DGM ITT-effect target (optional) ────────────────────────
# Under model = "null", k_treat scales the AFT log-time treatment
# coefficient.  k_treat = 1 preserves the fitted ITT effect (the
# default and the conservative choice).  If null_target_hr is
# non-NULL, k_treat is solved so the switched-scale ITT HR lands
# at the requested target -- useful for widening the gap from the
# c1 threshold when investigating type-I-error in isolation.  See
# the @sec-dgm-null section for the calculation and caveats.
null_target_hr    <- NULL   # e.g. 1.0 (no marginal effect) or 1.05

# ── Realistic analysis candidate set ─────────────────────────────
# Mirrors the binary vignette: a real analyst would NOT know which
# variables define Q nor where to cut them.  Continuous covariates are
# therefore supplied to forestsearch() and grf.subg.harm.survival() in
# their RAW form; the search methods discover cuts themselves
# (forestsearch: median / GRF-derived / forced cuts; GRF policy-tree
# splits).  The discretised z1-z12 variables are kept on the data
# frame only so generate_aft_dgm_flex() can build the super-population
# from them and so the truth column flag_harm can be checked --- they
# are NOT part of the analysis candidate set.
analysis_continuous_vars <- c(
  "age",      # continuous; TRUE cut (34) unknown to analyst
  "preanti",  # continuous; TRUE cut (744.5) unknown to analyst
  "wtkg",     # continuous
  "karnof",   # Karnofsky score (integer 70-100, treated as continuous)
  "cd40",     # baseline CD4 (continuous)
  "cd80"      # baseline CD8 (continuous)
)
analysis_binary_vars <- c(
  "hemo",     # hemophilia (0/1)
  "homo",     # homosexual activity (0/1)
  "drugs",    # IV drug use history (0/1)
  "race",     # race (0/1, white vs non-white as coded)
  "gender",   # gender (0/1)
  "symptom"   # symptomatic (0/1)
)

# ── Calibration ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Target HR(Q) = 2.0 under SWITCHED treatment (= 0.50 under original).
# This means the benefit subgroup has HR = 0.50 under the original
# treatment coding — a strong benefit.
cal_target_hr  <- 2.0
cal_k_grid     <- seq(1.0, 5.0, by = 0.25) # k_inter grid for grid search

# ── Single trial simulation ──────────────────────────────────────
single_n          <- 1000L  # Sample size for single-trial demonstration
single_seed       <- 1L     # Seed for single-trial demonstration
single_rand_ratio <- 1      # Randomisation ratio (1:1)

# ── Simulation study ─────────────────────────────────────────────
sim_n_sample      <- 1000L  # Per-simulation sample size
# Administrative censoring time on the DGM's time scale.
# CRITICAL: must use the SAME units as the outcome variable in the
# source data.  ACTG175 times are converted from days to months
# (days / 30.4375).
sim_analysis_time <- 48     # months 
sim_cens_adjust   <- 0      # Additional censoring adjustment (log-scale)
sim_n_noise       <- 0L     # Number of noise variables added per replicate

# ── Analysis flags ───────────────────────────────────────────────
run_fs      <- TRUE   # Run ForestSearch
run_fs_grf  <- FALSE  # Run ForestSearch with GRF pre-screening only
run_grf     <- TRUE   # Run GRF-only subgroup analysis

# ── ForestSearch parameters (benefit search thresholds) ─────────
# Under switched treatment roles, the thresholds are set to detect
# benefit on the ORIGINAL scale:
#   c1 = 1/0.60 ≈ 1.667: subgroup HR ≥ 1.667 (switched)
#                        = HR ≤ 0.60 (original)
#   c2 = 1/0.80 = 1.25:  split HRs ≥ 1.25 (switched)
#                        = HR ≤ 0.80 (original)
fs_hr_threshold        <- round(1 / 0.60, 3)  # c1 for benefit search
fs_hr_consistency      <- round(1 / 0.80, 3)  # c2 for benefit search
fs_pconsistency_thresh <- 0.90   # Bootstrap consistency proportion threshold
fs_splits              <- 400L   # Number of ForestSearch bootstrap splits
fs_n_min               <- 60L    # Minimum subgroup size (total)
fs_d0_min              <- 10L    # Minimum events in control arm
fs_d1_min              <- 10L    # Minimum events in treatment arm
fs_maxk                <- 2L     # Maximum number of subgroup-defining variables
fs_by_risk             <- 6L     # Risk-table interval (months)
fs_vi_grf_min          <- -0.2   # Minimum GRF variable importance

# ── GRF standalone parameters ───────────────────────────────────
# These control the GRF-only subgroup analysis (run_grf = TRUE).
# dmin.grf is on the RMST scale (months after time-unit conversion).
# The default in default_grf_params_gen() is dmin.grf = 12, which
# was calibrated for days (~0.4 months).  After converting ACTG175
# times to months, this must be rescaled.
grf_dmin               <- 2    # min RMST difference (months)
grf_frac_tau           <- 0.80   # fraction of max event time for horizon
grf_maxdepth           <- 2L     # max policy tree depth
grf_sg_criterion       <- "mDiff"
grf_tune               <- FALSE   # cross-validated GRF hyperparameter tuning
                                   # Set TRUE to enable tune.parameters = "all"

# ── Adjusted Cox formula (used in run_simulation_analysis) ───────
# Note: treat_sim is the SWITCHED treatment indicator in the
# simulated data.  Confounders z1 and z2 are the subgroup-
# defining variables; z3 is a strong prognostic covariate.
cox_formula_adj <- survival::Surv(y_sim, event_sim) ~
  treat_sim + z1 + z2 + z3

# ── Detection curve ──────────────────────────────────────────────
det_theta_range <- c(0.5, 3.0)  # HR range for detection curve
det_n_points    <- 50L          # Number of points on detection curve

# ── Results visualization ────────────────────────────────────────
# Controls for the subgroup-distribution and effect-distribution
# plots in @sec-results (rendered by forestsearch::plot_sg_distribution()
# and forestsearch::plot_effect_distribution()).  See the binary
# benefit vignette for a discussion of auto-halving and top-K behaviour.
sg_notation            <- "benefit"  # for effect-distribution inversion
sgdist_min_pct_alt     <- 5          # initial threshold, H1
sgdist_min_pct_null    <- 5          # initial threshold, H0
sgdist_top_k           <- 15L        # max bars before pooling
sgdist_show_other_alt  <- FALSE      # suppress pooled "Other" bar, H1
sgdist_show_other_null <- FALSE      # suppress pooled "Other" bar, H0

# -- Output persistence -------------------------------------------------------
# Save simulation results to _data/ for downstream analysis.
# Set save_results = FALSE to skip saving (e.g., during development).
save_results           <- TRUE
output_dir             <- "_data"
```


# Introduction {#sec-intro}

## Motivation

Leon et al. (2024) demonstrated the ForestSearch methodology using
the German Breast Cancer Study Group (GBSG) dataset
(`survival::gbsg`) as both the applied analysis target and the
covariate template for simulation studies.  The `setup_gbsg_dgm()`
convenience function encodes all GBSG-specific preparation choices
--- variable discretisation, subgroup definition, Weibull
calibration --- into a single reproducible call.

This document adapts the same simulation framework to the **AIDS
Clinical Trials Group Study 175** (ACTG175) dataset from the
`speff2trial` package.  ACTG175 is a randomised trial of four
antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected subjects (Hammer et al.,
*NEJM* 1996).  Following León et al. (2024, Section 4.2), we
compare **arm 1** (zidovudine + didanosine, ZDV+ddI) to **arm 3**
(didanosine alone, ddI) and search for a subgroup with
**pronounced treatment benefit** ($N = 1{,}083$).

The adaptation serves two purposes:

1. **Methodological validation**: confirming that the ForestSearch
   operating characteristics generalise beyond the GBSG breast
   cancer setting to a different disease, population, endpoint
   structure, and covariate set --- and specifically to the
   **benefit-search** variant of the algorithm.

2. **Template for new-dataset simulations**: demonstrating the
   recommended workflow when `setup_gbsg_dgm()` is not
   appropriate and the analyst must use
   `generate_aft_dgm_flex()` directly.


## Benefit Search via Treatment Switching {#sec-benefit-search}

ForestSearch's default mode identifies subgroups where treatment
is **detrimental** (hazard ratio $> 1$).  To identify subgroups
with **pronounced benefit** instead, León et al. (2024, §4.2)
introduced a treatment-switching approach:

1. **Switch treatment roles**: recode the treatment indicator so
   that control becomes "treatment" and vice versa.  In the
   ACTG175 context: ddI monotherapy (originally control) is
   recoded as `treat = 1`, and ZDV+ddI combination (originally
   experimental) becomes `treat = 0`.

2. **Raise the thresholds**: under switched roles, a subgroup
   that strongly benefits from the original treatment will appear
   to have a high HR (ddI alone is worse for these patients).
   The paper used:
   - $c_1 = 1/0.60 \approx 1.667$ (screening: original HR
     $\leq 0.60$)
   - $c_2 = 1/0.80 = 1.25$ (consistency: original HR
     $\leq 0.80$)

3. **Run ForestSearch** with these thresholds on the switched
   data.  The identified "harm" subgroup $\hat{H}$ under
   switched roles is the **benefit** subgroup $\hat{Q}$ under
   the original treatment coding.

4. **Invert the results**: hazard ratios reported by
   ForestSearch are inverted ($1/\text{HR}$) to return to the
   original treatment scale.

In the paper's analysis, this approach identified
$\hat{Q} = \{\text{Age} > 34 \cap \text{Preanti} \leq 744.5\}$
with a bias-corrected HR of $0.59$ ($0.37$, $0.94$) ---
a substantially stronger benefit than the ITT HR of $0.84$.

The simulation DGM in this document is built on the
**switched** treatment data.  All ForestSearch analyses run on
the switched indicator.  The calibration target HR $= 2.0$
(under switched treatment) corresponds to an original-scale
HR $= 0.50$, representing a strong treatment benefit in the
subgroup.


## Adaptation Checklist {#sec-checklist}

To substitute your own trial data for ACTG175, you must address
each of the following steps.  The sections that follow implement
each one for ACTG175; cross-references are provided so you can
see the concrete implementation alongside each checklist item.

| Step | What to do | Section |
|------|-----------|---------|
| **1. Load your data** | Create `id`, `y` (observed time), `event` (0/1 indicator), and `treat` (0 = control, 1 = treatment) columns. Time units for `y` set the time scale for the entire simulation. | @sec-comparison |
| **2. Choose confounders** | Identify the candidate variables for the subgroup search. These become `factor_vars` in the DGM and `confounders_base` in the simulation. | @sec-comparison |
| **3. Discretise continuous variables** | Create binary `z1`, `z2`, ... columns from continuous covariates. Document your cutpoint rationale (see @sec-cutpoints). | @sec-comparison |
| **4. Define the harm subgroup** | Set `dgm_subgroup_vars` and `dgm_subgroup_cuts` consistently with your factor coding. Verify with an explicit `stopifnot()` check. | @sec-dgm |
| **5. Set time-scale parameters** | Ensure `sim_analysis_time` is in the same units as your outcome variable. Run the time-scale diagnostic after DGM creation. | @sec-dgm |
| **6. Update `cox_formula_adj`** | Include confounders appropriate for your study. The formula must use simulated column names (`y_sim`, `event_sim`, `treat_sim`). | Setup chunk |
| **7. Update `confounders_base`** | This must list all `z*` variable names passed to ForestSearch and GRF. It must match `factor_vars` in the DGM call. | @sec-sims |
| **8. Calibrate `k_inter`** | Run the grid search targeting a clinically meaningful HR(H). | @sec-calibrate |
| **9. Run time-scale diagnostic** | Verify `exp(dgm$model_params$mu)` is close to your observed median event time. | @sec-timescale-check |
| **10. Run censoring diagnostic** | Use `check_censoring_dgm()` to compare simulated vs observed censoring. | @sec-cens-check |
| **11. Set simulation count** | Use $\geq 500$ replicates for stable operating characteristics. | @sec-sims |


## Choosing Discretisation Cutpoints {#sec-cutpoints}

ForestSearch operates on binary (factor) covariates.  Continuous
variables must be discretised before building the DGM.  There are
three common strategies:

1. **Clinical cutpoints** --- use thresholds defined by domain
   knowledge (e.g., CD4 $< 200$ cells/mm³ for AIDS-defining
   immunosuppression).  Preferred when available.

2. **Data-driven medians** --- split at the sample median;
   appropriate when no clinical threshold exists.  Used here
   for `z3` (Karnofsky performance score) and `z4` (CD4
   baseline count).

3. **GRF-guided splits** --- run a preliminary GRF analysis on the
   observed data (`grf::causal_forest()`) to identify the
   variable-importance-weighted split points that maximise
   treatment effect heterogeneity.  This was the approach for
   `z1` (age $> 34$) and `z2` (preanti $\leq 744.5$), derived from
   the analysis in `actg175_analysis_v1.Rnw`.

For your own dataset, we recommend starting with strategy (1)
where available, falling back to (2), and optionally using (3) as
a sensitivity analysis.  Whichever approach you choose, document
the rationale alongside the cutpoint value in your setup chunk.


## Steps for Swapping GBSG with ACTG175 {#sec-swap-steps}

Replacing the GBSG template with ACTG175 requires changes at every
stage of the simulation pipeline.  The table below summarises each
change; subsequent sections implement them in detail.

| Step | GBSG (original) | ACTG175 (this document) |
|------|-----------------|-------------------------|
| **Data source** | `survival::gbsg` (686 patients) | `speff2trial::ACTG175`, arms 1 vs 3 (~1,083 patients) |
| **Outcome** | Recurrence-free survival in months (`rfstime / 30.4375`) | Time to first event in months (`days / 30.4375`) |
| **Event indicator** | `status` (1 = recurrence/death) | `cens` (1 = event) |
| **Treatment** | `hormon` (0/1) | `arms`: 1 = ZDV+ddI (combination), 3 = ddI (monotherapy); **switched** for benefit search |
| **Confounders** | 7 binary variables: ER, age, meno, PgR, nodes, size, grade | 12 variables: age, preanti, weight, Karnofsky, CD4, CD8, hemophilia, homosexual, IV drugs, race, gender, symptoms |
| **Discretisation** | ER $\leq$ Q25, age $\leq$ median, meno = premenopausal, etc. | Age $>$ 34, preanti $\leq$ 744.5, weight $\leq$ 75 kg, CD4 $\leq$ median, etc. (from León et al. 2024 analysis) |
| **Subgroup definition** | *H* = {ER-low and premenopausal} (~13% prevalence) | *Q* = {Age > 34 and Preanti ≤ 744.5} (~35% prevalence, benefit subgroup) || **DGM builder** | `setup_gbsg_dgm()` | `generate_aft_dgm_flex()` |
| **Censoring** | Weibull; `analysis_time = 84` months | Weibull; `analysis_time = 48` months ($\sim$4 years) |
| **ForestSearch parameters** | `n.min = 60`, `maxk = 2`, `hr.threshold = 1.25` | `hr.threshold = 1.667`, `hr.consistency = 1.25` (benefit search thresholds) |

The benefit subgroup definition for ACTG175 is derived from the
ForestSearch analysis in León et al. (2024, Section 4.2), which
identified Age $> `r actg_age_cut`$ and prior antiretroviral
therapy $\leq `r actg_preanti_cut`$ days as the combination
defining a subgroup with pronounced treatment benefit
($\hat{Q}$: HR $= 0.59$, $0.37$--$0.94$).

```{r compat-helper}
#| include: false
# Backward-compatibility aliases for generate_aft_dgm_flex() objects.
# Several downstream functions (build_classification_table, etc.)
# access top-level fields (hr_H_true, df_super_rand) that exist on
# gbsg_dgm objects but not on native aft_dgm_flex objects.  This
# helper adds the aliases so the pipeline works with either DGM type.
add_compat_aliases <- function(dgm) {
  if (is.null(dgm$hr_H_true) && !is.null(dgm$hazard_ratios)) {
    dgm$hr_H_true  <- dgm$hazard_ratios$harm_subgroup
    dgm$hr_Hc_true <- dgm$hazard_ratios$no_harm_subgroup
    dgm$hr_causal  <- dgm$hazard_ratios$overall
    dgm$AHR        <- dgm$hazard_ratios$AHR
    dgm$AHR_H_true <- dgm$hazard_ratios$AHR_harm
    dgm$AHR_Hc_true <- dgm$hazard_ratios$AHR_no_harm
  }
  if (is.null(dgm$df_super_rand) && !is.null(dgm$df_super)) {
    dgm$df_super_rand <- dgm$df_super
  }
  dgm
}
```


## Loading and Preparing Both Datasets

The code below prepares both datasets for the simulation framework.
For each dataset, the key steps are:

1. Create a standardised outcome variable (`y`) in the dataset's
   natural time units.
2. Create a binary treatment indicator (`treat`: 0 = control,
   1 = treatment).
3. Discretise continuous covariates into binary factors
   (`z1`, `z2`, ...) using the cutpoints defined in the setup
   chunk.
4. Construct the true harm-subgroup indicator (`flag_harm`)
   using the same variables and levels specified in
   `dgm_subgroup_vars` and `dgm_subgroup_cuts`.

```{r prepare-datasets}
#| code-fold: false

# ── GBSG ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
gbsg_df        <- survival::gbsg
gbsg_df$y      <- gbsg_df$rfstime / 30.4375
gbsg_df$treat  <- gbsg_df$hormon

er_cut         <- quantile(gbsg_df$er, probs = gbsg_er_quantile)
gbsg_df$z1     <- as.factor(ifelse(gbsg_df$er <= er_cut, 1L, 0L))
gbsg_df$z3     <- as.factor(ifelse(gbsg_df$meno == 0, 1L, 0L))
gbsg_df$flag_harm <- as.integer(gbsg_df$z1 == 1 & gbsg_df$z3 == 1)

# ── ACTG175 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Select arms 1 (ZDV+ddI) and 3 (ddI alone), matching the paper
actg_df        <- subset(speff2trial::ACTG175, arms %in% actg_arms)
actg_df$id     <- seq_len(nrow(actg_df))
actg_df$time_days   <- actg_df$days
actg_df$time_months <- actg_df$time_days / 30.4375

# Original treatment coding: arm 1 (ZDV+ddI) = 1, arm 3 (ddI) = 0
actg_df$treat_orig <- ifelse(actg_df$arms == actg_treat_arm, 1L, 0L)

# SWITCHED treatment coding for benefit search:
# ddI (arm 3) = 1 ("treatment"), ZDV+ddI (arm 1) = 0 ("control")
# Under switched roles, ForestSearch's harm-detection machinery
# identifies the BENEFIT subgroup Q.
actg_df$treat  <- 1L - actg_df$treat_orig

cat(sprintf("ACTG175: N = %d (arm 1: n=%d, arm 3: n=%d)\n",
    nrow(actg_df),
    sum(actg_df$treat_orig == 1), sum(actg_df$treat_orig == 0)))
cat(sprintf("Treatment switched: treat=1 is ddI (original control)\n"))

# ── Discretise continuous variables into binary factors ───────
# Subgroup-defining variables (from Leon et al. 2024, Section 4.2):
# z1: age > actg_age_cut  (subgroup factor 1 — older patients)
actg_df$z1  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$age  > actg_age_cut,  1L, 0L))
# z2: preanti <= actg_preanti_cut  (subgroup factor 2 — less prior treatment)
actg_df$z2  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$preanti <= actg_preanti_cut, 1L, 0L))
# z3: weight <= actg_wtkg_cut (prognostic)
actg_df$z3  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$wtkg <= actg_wtkg_cut, 1L, 0L))
# z4: Karnofsky <= median (data-driven cutpoint)
actg_df$z4  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$karnof <= median(actg_df$karnof), 1L, 0L
))
# z5: CD4 baseline <= median (data-driven cutpoint)
actg_df$z5  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$cd40 <= median(actg_df$cd40), 1L, 0L
))
# z6: CD8 <= median (data-driven cutpoint)
actg_df$z6  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$cd80 <= median(actg_df$cd80), 1L, 0L
))
# z7-z12: binary indicators (passed through as-is from the dataset)
actg_df$z7  <- as.factor(actg_df$hemo)
actg_df$z8  <- as.factor(actg_df$homo)
actg_df$z9  <- as.factor(actg_df$drugs)
actg_df$z10 <- as.factor(actg_df$race)
actg_df$z11 <- as.factor(actg_df$gender)
actg_df$z12 <- as.factor(actg_df$symptom)

# ── Realistic analyst-facing candidate set ──────────────────────
# The truly-binary indicators are coerced to factors so forestsearch's
# is.continuous() detection treats them as categorical (no median /
# GRF cut attempted).  The continuous columns (age, preanti, wtkg,
# karnof, cd40, cd80) are left in their RAW numeric form -- the
# search methods discover cuts.  The z1-z12 factors built above
# remain on the data frame only for the DGM (factor_vars argument)
# and the truth flag.
for (v in analysis_binary_vars) {
  actg_df[[v]] <- as.factor(actg_df[[v]])
}
confounders_analysis <- c(analysis_continuous_vars, analysis_binary_vars)

# ── Factor coding summary ──────────────────────────────────────
# z1  = 1 => age > 34          (older — benefit subgroup factor)
# z2  = 1 => preanti <= 744.5  (less prior ART — benefit subgroup factor)
# z3  = 1 => weight <= 75 kg   (low weight)
# z4  = 1 => Karnofsky <= median (lower performance)
# z5  = 1 => CD4 <= median     (lower baseline CD4)
# z6  = 1 => CD8 <= median     (lower CD8)
# z7  = 1 => hemophilia yes
# z8  = 1 => homosexual activity yes
# z9  = 1 => IV drug use yes
# z10 = 1 => non-white
# z11 = 1 => male
# z12 = 1 => symptomatic yes

# ── Benefit subgroup: z1 = 1 AND z2 = 1 ───────────────────────
# Q = {Age > 34 AND Preanti <= 744.5}
# Under switched treatment, Q appears as the "harm" subgroup.
actg_df$flag_harm <- as.integer(
  actg_df[[dgm_subgroup_vars[1]]] == dgm_subgroup_cuts[[dgm_subgroup_vars[1]]] &
  actg_df[[dgm_subgroup_vars[2]]] == dgm_subgroup_cuts[[dgm_subgroup_vars[2]]]
)

# Verify subgroup definition matches expectations
stopifnot(
  identical(dgm_subgroup_vars, c("z1", "z2")),
  identical(dgm_subgroup_cuts, list(z1 = 1L, z2 = 1L))
)
cat(sprintf(
  "Benefit subgroup Q: z1 == 1 (age > %d) AND z2 == 1 (preanti <= %.1f)\n",
  actg_age_cut, actg_preanti_cut
))
cat(sprintf(
  "  Q prevalence: %d / %d (%.1f%%)\n",
  sum(actg_df$flag_harm), nrow(actg_df),
  100 * mean(actg_df$flag_harm)
))
```
